stories.body:
Host city offers showcase of China’s rise into a confident and innovative power central to global economy

I n a Shenzhen square on a balmy evening, locals and tourists watched the dozens of glinting towers that make up the city’s skyline ripple through the colour spectrum – cyan and violet, cyber green, China’s national scarlet and gold – repeatedly flashing the words “Apec 2026”.

The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is a dream showcase for one of China’s most advanced cities, and the country’s leader, Xi Jinping , is basking in its neon glow.

On the sidelines, a series of high-profile bilateral meetings and the announcement of a historic three-way summit with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have cemented Xi’s status as an agenda setter on the global stage.

The broader Apec summit , meanwhile, provides an opportunity for China to present itself as a steward of multilateralism against what it terms “unilateralism and protectionism” – that is to say, trade measures taken against Beijing by countries such as the US.

All this is set against the futuristic backdrop that is Shenzhen, a city that perhaps better than no other embodies China’s rise into a confident, technologically innovative power central to the global economy.

A photo display in the Apec media centre charts Shenzhen’s transformation from sparsely populated marshland, calling it “a miracle in the history of world development created by the Chinese people”.

“[Xi] wants people to go home Chinamaxxing,” said Prof Astrid Nordin, of King’s College London. “Shenzhen is itself part of the message. It’s a showcase of Chinese technological and economic achievements, and of China’s claim that it offers opportunities for prosperity in a world increasingly characterised by uncertainty and conflict.”

Like the light show, the summit is being carefully coordinated. The Financial Times cited people familiar with the matter as saying it would be one of the most tightly controlled in the organisation’s history, with leaders having to travel to a state guesthouse beside Shenzhen’s tiger safari park to meet Xi. The paper said diplomats had grumbled that the format “seems designed to reduce the free-flowing discussion characteristic of prior editions”.

Setting out its expectations for the summit, China’s foreign ministry has said it looks forward to “practical results in key areas such as trade, connectivity, digital economy, AI and so on”.

Already, Xi has announced trade wins with Canada’s Mark Carney, extending remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products by two years in exchange for tariff relief on Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports.

A meeting with Papua New ⁠Guinea’s leader, meanwhile, showed how Beijing’s geopolitical priorities have been absorbed and reflected by its allies, with James Marape recounting to Xi how he had closed Taiwan’s office in his country despite domestic challenges in doing so.

The most important meeting will be between Xi and Trump. The leaders of the world’s two superpowers are expected to tackle a broad range of issues including AI and trade. In a move that could strain the fragile tariff truce that the two leaders first agreed last year, the Trump administration said on Monday it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips.

Christopher Adams, a senior adviser at the law firm Covington who was at the centre of trade negotiations with China for the Obama and first Trump administrations, said: “The trade truce may increasingly look like a ceasefire in a war where major combat operations remain on hold but skirmishes are escalating to the point where the line between peace and war is blurred.

“I don’t see pressure to announce a further extension of the trade truce in Shenzhen. If a significant extension is announced, that would be an upside surprise.”

China has not hesitated to leverage Apec’s multinational platform in service of its arguments. A commentary by the state news agency Xinhua on Tuesday said: “Amid deepening geopolitical rivalries and growing global divisions, [China’s hosting] sends a clear signal that great-power competition need not be a zero-sum game, and that one country’s development need not come at the expense of another.”

The chair of the Apec senior officials’ meeting, Chen Xu, said Beijing had made trade “openness” a key focus of its Apec year and looked forward to “achieving more practical outcomes on the trade front”.

The much anticipated trilateral summit with Trump and Putin, on the other hand, could prove largely symbolic. For Xi, “it provides the appearance of China shaping the world order as an equal to the United States,” said Dr Kevork Oskanian, an expert on Russia at the University of Exeter. “Agreement on substantial issues, which would, in any case, require extensive preparatory negotiations, is unlikely.”

For China’s ruling Communist party, the political pomp has another key purpose. Nordin said summits were “occasions for leaders to tell stories about the world, about their country’s place in it … and one of the most important audiences for those stories is at home.”

For the locals watching the skyscraper light show on Monday night, the symbolism was not lost. China’s export might had helped it become increasingly powerful on the world stage, said one local man, who did not give his name. “It’s so great that the summit will take place in Shenzhen,” he said. “I feel very proud.”

stories.title: Robo-soldier startup backed by Eric Trump misses payroll, may collapse
stories.summary: Robotics startup misses payroll a year after CEO used funds for luxury home.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Robotics startup misses payroll a year after CEO used funds for luxury home.

A humanoid robotics company backed and advised by President Donald Trump’s son, Eric Trump, has reportedly missed payroll and may be on the brink of collapse after a funding shortfall. The Silicon Valley startup, Foundation Future Industries, claims it is developing and testing robots for military roles on battlefields from Ukraine to Gaza.

Foundation failed to pay employees for the payroll period ending on October 30, anonymous sources told CNBC . The startup’s staff is especially angry because Foundation’s co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak , supposedly borrowed $4.6 million in company funds to buy a luxury home overlooking San Francisco Bay about a year ago.

This comes as Pathak and Foundation’s leadership are still looking to raise funding to support a $3 billion valuation, based on their promise to develop a humanoid robot ready for combat duty and capable of wielding various weapons.

The company has demonstrated a humanoid robot named the Phantom MK-1 and is touting an upcoming robot called the Phantom MK-2. Foundation has touted its humanoid robots for roles in warehouses and other workplaces—but has courted media coverage by claiming it is developing humanoid robots for battlefield use.

Now CNBC’s reporting based on “people with direct knowledge of the matter” indicates that insiders worry the startup could soon collapse without additional funding.

Foundation’s business claims

Eric Trump holds an equity stake in Foundation and was announced as its chief strategy advisor in March 2026, according to the Financial Times . Investment funds linked to both Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. are involved with multiple military technology companies that have received Pentagon loans and contracts worth more than $3.2 billion as of July 2026, according to The Washington Post .

After Trump claimed that Foundation had “just secured a $24 million contract with the Pentagon” during the Fox Business interview in April, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) responded by questioning whether the Pentagon is “just a cash machine from Trump’s kids now” in a social media post . “This looks like corruption in plain sight,” Warren wrote.

But publicly available evidence does not back up Trump’s claim about Foundation directly receiving US government funding. Federal spending records show that Foundation holds no publicly listed contracts, according to The San Francisco Standard .

Instead, the company Boardwalk Robotics received four contracts worth $3.22 million prior to being acquired by Foundation in late 2024.

Meanwhile, the Institute for Human & Machine Cognition—a Florida-based nonprofit research institute and research partner to Boardwalk Robotics—secured a $24.8 million Navy contract in 2025, The San Francisco Standard reported.

This was not the first time that Foundation’s leadership and investors have made unsupported statements. In 2024, General Motors pushed back on Foundation’s claims that it was about to get an investment from the Detroit automaker, according to CNBC .

Shaky battlefield testing claims

On November 11, 2026, Mike LeBlanc, co-founder and president of Foundation Future Industries, told the Financial Times that the company was in talks with the Israeli military to provide humanoid robots for patrol and combat duties in Hamas tunnels beneath Gaza. He also described taking the company’s Phantom MK1 humanoid robot along to tour some of the tunnels.

However, the Israeli defense ministry declined to comment when the Financial Times reached out.

LeBlanc also previously claimed that two of the company’s Phantom MK-1 units went to Ukraine for testing in frontline reconnaissance and logistics roles in February 2026.

But Craig Smith , an independent journalist and host of the podcast Eye on AI , described tagging along during the delivery of the Phantom robots to Ukraine. He said that the robots never made it to Ukraine because they were stopped at the border with Poland.

When questioned by Smith, LeBlanc only said that Foundation had conducted a pilot demonstration at an undisclosed location, without clarifying whether the robots ever reached Ukraine. LeBlanc also walked back a claim that Foundation had demonstrated its humanoid robots to the Ukrainian government organization Brave1.

Promotional videos showing Foundation’s humanoids have not provided evidence that the robots are ready for battlefield deployments. For example, a “mortar demo” video on the company website dated to May 2026 shows a person handing a mortar shell to one of the humanoid robots, which slowly lowers the shell over the muzzle of a mortar weapon before finally dropping it in.

The real battlefield robots

Whatever happens to Foundation, humanoid robots remain largely unproven technology and have yet to fulfill company promises that they can become general-purpose robots handling many different tasks. Companies have just begun testing and deploying such robots in greater numbers within relatively controlled environments such as factories and warehouses.

Similarly, humanoid robots have not yet had any impact on the battlefield. Instead, pioneers in robotics warfare such as the Ukrainian military have focused on developing and deploying unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs)—robotic vehicles that roll along on wheels or tank-style caterpillar tracks.

While defending against the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the Ukrainian military has increasingly deployed more ground robots along with swarms of flying drones to make up for a shortfall in human soldiers compared to Russia. Such ground robots have typically been tasked with performing risky supply runs or evacuating wounded soldiers from frontline positions, but have also entered combat while wielding projectile weapons or even explosives when equipped as roving bombs.

Most recently, Ukraine has deployed armed ground robots directly into combat through both amphibious landings and through airdrops . In 2026, part of Ukraine’s counteroffensive success in rolling back Russian territorial gains has included dropping military robots from drones in airborne assaults behind Russian frontline positions.

stories.title: US government confirms investigation into tech firm Megaspeed
stories.summary: The Singapore-based company is suspected of helping to ship high-end AI chips from tech giant Nvidia to China, violating US export rules.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 2 hours ago

The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia's chips to China.

In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.

It comes after questions were raised about the possibility high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

Concerns emerged in recent weeks after Nvidia founder Jensen Huang revealed he had an extramarital affair , allegedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. US authorities suspect her of spying for Beijing, which China denies.

Jensen Huang resigned from his role as chief executive last week following revelations he had two affairs.

Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.

The justice and commerce departments said on Monday that "it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information" regarding the investigation.

Laying out a timeline, it said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".

In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia "concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed". In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list.

Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, then conducted an on-site check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was chief executive at the time.

Alice Huang and Jensen Huang pictured together in Taiwan in June 2024

Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.

The Nvidia scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end chips to Megaspeed.

On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of the chips.

Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.

While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.

Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.

The White House said on Monday it would further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.

The reported affairs by Jensen Huang created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a major company in the AI industry and central to the US as it competes with China for dominance.

Trump downplays warnings of AI risks, citing rivalry with China

In the statement, the US government said it would "bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred".

They added: "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the US economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge."

China slams new US chip curbs and pledges 'necessary measures'

China has threatened to retaliate against the US after Washington tightened restrictions on remote access to AI chips and servers.

At a press conference on Tuesday, China’s foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Beijing would take “necessary measures” to safeguard its own interests, saying:

double quotation mark “The US has repeatedly overstretched the concept of national security, abused export controls and even interfered in China’s normal trade and technological cooperation with other countries, unjustifiably suppressing the development of China’s high-tech industries.”

Guo also called the US move a typical example of economic coercion that deviates from the consensus reached by both countries, Reuters reports .

As we blogged yesterday , the US Commerce Department has issued a new rule which limits remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips by companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil.

The new measure closes a loophole which allowed Chinese companies to access cutting-edge US tech by using data centres based in other countries in Asia.

Awkwardly for Beijing, the new “interim final rule” is being imposed just as Donald Trump prepares to meet China’s president Xi Jinping later this week in Shenzhen, which is hosting this week’s APEC summit.

Dexter Roberts , a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Global China Hub, says ( via Bloomberg ):

double quotation mark “This is the worst situation possible for China because the last thing they want to see is any new restrictions on their access to chips.” “Export controls are what upset them practically more than anything else right now other than maybe Taiwan.”

Sentiment towards Nvidia has improved slightly!

Its shares are now up 1% in premarket trading at $157.85, on track to recover around a quarter of yesterday’s losses.

US government confirms investigation into Megaspeed over Nvidia chip exports

Two US government departments have confirmed they are investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia’s chips to China.

A joint statement issued by the Department of Commerce and the Department of Justice explains that Megaspeed has been under investigation since 2024, for “potential export control violations.”

In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list, they explain.

And they also state that commerce department agents conducted an on-site, in-person, end-use check at Megaspeed in June 2025 and interviewed CEO Alice Huang.

The Department of Justice then took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.

Tooting their own trumpets, the departments add:

double quotation mark This investigation is the result of the excellent work of the Department of Commerce under Secretary Howard Lutnick and the law enforcement efforts of the Department of Justice under Attorney General Todd Blanche.

That, presumably, is a response to suggestions that Lutnick could be fired following accusations that he had shielded Nvidia from federal oversight, and had failed to blacklist Megaspeed.

US ⁠President ⁠Donald Trump has said that Nvidia’s new national ⁠security initiative is a good idea, while speaking in Manila.

Nvidia establishes National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee

Nvidia has announced it is creating a new committee to oversee its national security policies, check it is complying with export controls and manage its global trade risk effectively.

The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee demonstrates that Nvidia is committed to “the highest standards of governance and oversight,” the company says.

It’s a response to claims that billions of dollars worth of the company’s top AI chips have been redirected to China.

Harvey Jones , chairman of Nvidia’s board of directors.

double quotation mark “NVIDIA recognizes that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security. As the world’s leading advanced computing company, NVIDIA has both a responsibility and an opportunity to lead the industry in addressing these challenges. We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation.”

Investors’ euphoria over the AI boom is over, according to the latest survey of fund managers from Bank of America.

BofA’s monthly poll has found that investors have slashed their technology holdings this month. The percentage of investors who were ‘overweight’ on tech stocks fell at the fastest rate since 2006 in November.

The survey also found that 38% of investors predicted that bonds issued by AI hyperscalers are the most likely source of a credit event, followed by private credit with 30%.

BofA investment strategist Michael Hartnett says investors remain bullish on the macro-economic front, with just 3% predicting a recession. They are also optimistic about markets, with cash holdings at an “uber-low 3.6%”.

EU charges Temu with illegal items failints

Newsflash: The European Commission has charged online shopping retailer Temu with failing to tackle the sale of illegal products, my colleague Jennifer Rankin reports.

The EU regulator found that the Chinese online shopping website did not have effective controls to prevent the sale of illegal items, thereby breaching the EU’s Digital Services Act.

Temu has been contacted for comment. The company now has the right to see the charge sheet and mount a defence.

The charges, announced on Tuesday, come after a €200m (£173m) fine on Temu from the EU in May on the grounds of inadequate risk assessment in 2024 to prevent the sale of illegal products and recommender systems that could amplify the promotion of such items.

The latest charges were brought under a different article of the EU’s Digital Services Act, which is intended to protect European internet users from online harms ranging from disinformation to cyberbullying to dangerous goods. They also relate to harms over a longer period, dating since the relevant provisions came into effect in October 2024.

Commission officials said Temu’s “ineffective” controls to stop illegal goods focused on paperwork, rather than products. It also found there were not enough human moderators to manage the huge growth in items listed on the platform. Third-party sellers offering illegal products, EU officials said, faced only weak sanctions from Temu and company systems enabled repeat offenders to sell through other parts of its website.

Temu has 130m users in the EU. If the charges are upheld Temu could be fined 6% of its global annual turnover.

The company said in May it disagreed with the Commission’s decision and saw the €200m fine as disproportionate.

The Commission examined Temu’s risk management systems, rather than specific products. Consumer groups in the EU and UK have previously reported that Temu has offered for sale baby toys presenting choking hazards, jewellery laced with dangerous metals including lead, clothes made with banned chemicals and illegal weapons.

Singapore has said it is carefully studying the new US clampdown on Chinese companies renting computing power from data centres powered by Nvidia chips, in countries including Singapore.

The Singaporean government has said:

double quotation mark “We take our international reputation seriously and do not condone companies using their association with Singapore to circumvent or violate the laws of other countries in their international business activities, including export controls.

The scandal “is obviously not a good look for Singapore“, Chong Ja Ian , a political scientist with the National University of Singapore , told the AFP newswire.

Singapore is also probing what Megaspeed was up to, but Chong said the city-state must strengthen regulatory oversight to avoid the perception of “systemic issues”.

Concerns that the AI boom may slow is pushing down the copper price today.

Copper has fallen to its lowest level in four and a half months, touching $13,144 a metric ton on the London Metal Exchange this morning.

Copper is heavily used in the AI industry – both to build data centre infrasctructure, and to cool the systems. It is also essential in power networks.

The US president, Donald Trump , has arrived in Manila, the capital of the Philippines, for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit,.

After departing from the Boeing 747 gifted to him by Qatar, Trump was greeted by officials and members of the military on the red carpet laid out on the Ninoy Aquino International Airport’s tarmac.

My colleague Yohannes Lowe is blogging all the key developments:

Demonstrators have also gathered in Manila to protest against Trump:

After a tough day yesterday, when they fell over 4%, Nvidia’s shares on track to dip further.

Nvidia’s shares are down 0.5% in premarket trading, ahead of their latest financial results tonight.

Daniela Hathorn , senior market analyst at capital,com , says:

double quotation mark Investors are expecting revenue of around $109bn, but the focus will be on data-centre demand, margins, forward guidance and reassurance about the company’s leadership transition. Strong results could help restore confidence in the AI sector, although even an earnings beat may not be enough if management fails to address concerns about future investment returns. Conversely, disappointing guidance could accelerate the selloff.

European stock markets are down across the board today, after a weak session in the Asia-Pacific.

The pan-European Stoxx 600 index is down 0.9%, with losses on the main indices in Frankfurt (-1%), Paris (-1%), Madrid (-0.5%) and Milan (-0.6%) as well as London (-0.8%).

Overnight, South Korea’s Kospi index dropped by another 2.6% as stocks linked to the AI sector continued to be hit.

AJ Bell investment director Russ Mould says:

double quotation mark “Despite its limited exposure to AI, the UK market could not entirely shake off the negative sentiment in markets as tech stocks chalked up further losses,” says “Asian markets experienced further weakness and London’s contingent of heavyweight resources stocks also came under pressure as commodity prices eased. “While US futures are pointing to a steady start on Wall Street later, the tone for the remainder of the week will hinge on Nvidia’s earnings update after the bell.

The US has added “another layer of regulatory risk to the global AI trade” by tightening restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI computing through overseas data centres, says Charu Chanana , chief investment strategist at Saxo .

In a new research note, Chanana explains:

China AI is no longer one trade. Domestic semiconductor suppliers could benefit from the self-sufficiency push, while AI developers face higher costs and potentially slower innovation.

Nvidia and US tech face indirect risks. Nvidia’s reported China revenue may not fully capture demand routed through overseas data centres. The bigger question is how restrictions affect future AI infrastructure orders.

Could regulation become the next big AI risk? Restrictions could eventually extend beyond chips and computing access to Chinese AI models. That could raise costs for businesses using cheaper Chinese models and slow AI adoption — the phase where we expect broader economic value to emerge.

Tension rises ahead of Nvidia's results tonoight

Any set of financial results from Nvidia are important, but there’s particular excitement in the markets today before the chip giant publishes its third-quarter results after Wall Street trading ends tonight.

Nvidia’s Q3 results, and the subsequent conference call with analysts and investors, will be very closely scrutinised given the crisis gripping the company .

Nvidia’s future forecasts will be a key measure of whether the AI industry is growing as rapidly as forecast.

But it will also, surely, be quizzed over the resignation of Jensen Huang last week. Will the board confirm that there is no chance of a return for Huang, who quit after reports of extramarital liaisons, including with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang ?

Interim CEO Colette Kress could also face questions about reports that $12bn of Nvidia’s chips were directed to companies in China by Megaspeed, Alice Huang’s company.

Kress might also be quizzed about reports that she is concerned about Nvidia’s web of financial support for AI companies….

Investors may also wonder whether the latest clampdown on remote access to AI chips – which have irked China – will hurt Nvidia’s sales.

Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB, explains:

double quotation mark The question is, can they calm investors’ nerves about the AI trade? The market expects another monster report. Expectations are for revenue to come in above $109bn for last quarter, a jump of 92% on a YoY basis, earnings per share is expected at $2.47. There is no reason to think that Nvidia will miss these figures, and based on the recent trend of their results, they are likely to post sales figures above expectations. Although profit margins could dip to 73% from 74%, the company is still likely to report a bullet proof balance sheet, with over $180bn in free cash flow. Nearly all AI companies use Nvidia chips, so the question is: will export restrictions to Asian countries that have acted as conduits to China have a material impact on the company’s revenues going forward?

stories.title: Government must act now or lose Royal Mail, former minister warns
stories.summary: The former business secretary says "undercutting" by rivals will make Royal Mail "unviable".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 17 November 2026, 11:54 GMT

Former Business Secretary Peter Kyle has said the government must act urgently to "level the playing field" for Royal Mail or risk the business becoming unviable.

He said he was concerned that the firm was being "undercut" by rival parcel delivery firms who did not employ staff under the same conditions.

Royal Mail, which is owned by International Distribution Services, has struggled in recent years with increased competition, fewer letters being sent and fines from the regulator for missing delivery targets.

A government spokesperson said it would consider whether further reforms are required to the parcel market after the watchdog, Ofcom, publishes its annual monitoring report in December.

Kyle had started to prepare officials at the Department for Business and Trade (DBT) to look at the delivery market for parcels shortly before he was replaced in his job by Jonathan Reynolds as business secretary in July.

He said a "crunch point" had been reached where the government had to make a decision about whether it wants Royal Mail "to be a viable proposition in the future".

He said his review would have looked at where the costs in that market lay and where the profit was being made, to see successful companies upheld "the values of business in Britain today".

"If we leave it another few years then Royal Mail will just become unviable and it will just collapse under the weight of having full-time employees," he said.

According to Royal Mail, 98% of its 130,000 workers are permanent employees, with rights to benefits including pensions, sick pay and holiday pay.

Some other parcel delivery companies use self-employed delivery drivers, with some offering an opt-in service that gives couriers limited additional benefits.

Royal Mail is also legally obliged to offer customers a "one price goes anywhere" service across the UK and to deliver first class letters six days a week to every address.

Kyle's proposed review would not have considered further changes to Royal Mail's universal service obligations or to terms and conditions for its staff.

Former Business Secretary Peter Kyle had planned to launch a review of the parcel delivery market

Royal Mail's performance has improved in recent months but it is still missing its targets for delivering first and second class post.

The firm was fined £21m in October 2025 for missing delivery targets in 2024/25.

Ofcom agreed last year to scrap second class deliveries on Saturdays and to reduce the target for delivering first class post within a day of collection to 90%.

A government spokesperson said the current business secretary had met Royal Mail and the Communication Workers Union, which represents postal workers, last week "to seek timely progress on improving their quality of service and to reiterate our commitment to the company's success."

DBT has also launched a consultation on tackling , external what it calls "bogus" self-employment, which it describes as "a practice whereby some businesses mislabel staff as self-employed to avoid statutory obligations".

Royal Mail has welcomed the consultation, and a spokesperson for the company claimed some parts of the delivery industry were "driving a race to the bottom" on employment standards and said it would "continue to push for a level playing field, with strong and enforceable standards across the industry."

Royal Mail misses delivery targets again but hails 'encouraging' signs Published 21 August

Hundreds of Royal Mail staff quitting each week under new efficiency plans Published 14 October

Many MPs across the UK have reported receiving high volumes of complaints from constituents about missed and delayed deliveries.

Shadow business minister Bradley Thomas said that Royal Mail's management needed to address the business's failings.

"Customers are being asked time and time again to pay increased prices, yet the service they're receiving is not improving," he said.

"Be in no doubt, this is not the fault of the hardworking postmen and women, it's the fault of Royal Mail's management.

"Nationalisation isn't the solution to this problem. Instead, we need ministers and Ofcom to bear down on Royal Mail's management to ensure they deliver on the improvements they've promised their customers."

The Communication Workers Union, which represents Royal Mail workers, is also putting pressure on ministers, with General Secretary Dave Ward calling for a "new model of ownership".

stories.title: US moves to cut China’s remote access to AI chips
stories.summary: Trump bets China won’t mind US blocking remote access to AI chips.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Trump bets China won’t mind US blocking remote access to AI chips.

On the heels of the Nvidia scandal , the Trump administration is preparing to crack down on foreign data centers that are fueling China’s advancements in artificial intelligence by allowing remote access to otherwise restricted high-end chips necessary for AI training.

In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department said it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil.

US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department said. Among threats, the US fears rivals could use advanced AI to develop “more effective weapons of mass destruction and advanced conventional weapons, coordinated cyber-espionage and targeted cyber-disruption, algorithmic theft, and weaponized disinformation.”

Now, the rules have been tightened up so much that the South China Morning Post reported that, “as a result, any advanced chips made for a Chinese firm are assumed to be restricted, and factories must ask the US government for a license before shipping them.”

The rule change takes effect 90 days after it’s posted to the Federal Register. Moving forward, companies headquartered in any of those countries deemed to “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to China, Russia, and Iran must apply for a license with strict know-your-customer controls when transferring high volumes of advanced chips. If a license is granted, companies will have to “perform robust due diligence,” submitting monthly reports on transactions that thoroughly detail all parties involved, as well as their parent companies, and the final destination for chips sold.

In a press release Sunday, the Commerce Department described the rule change as “designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries.” An exception was carved out for companies providing computing power “exclusively used for commercial recommender systems.” The Department said it was acting to “prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests.”

Without the intervention, officials fear that China could develop a military or economic edge, The New York Times reported .

Trump officials clash on new rule

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to an affair with a woman, Alice Huang, suspected of serving as a Chinese spy . Congress is probing if Alice Huang used her personal relationship with Jensen Huang to help her former company, Megaspeed, become one of Nvidia’s biggest customers, then used that position to smuggle Nvidia’s restricted AI chips into China. China has denied that Alice Huang was a spy, and Megaspeed has denied that smuggling occurred, while launching its own internal probe.

Megaspeed is a Singaporean data center firm whose primary business is cloud computing and AI infrastructure. Prior to the rule change, selling remote access to AI servers to customers in China was perfectly legal, NYT noted. But now, the Commerce Department has given firms like Megaspeed 90 days to either obtain licenses or face future export restrictions.

Whether or not to add more chip curbs has been a polarizing debate in the Trump administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly butted heads with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. When the Megaspeed news broke, Bessent pushed for curbs, but Lutnick reportedly appeared “too cozy” with Nvidia to move. Instead, Lutnick initially favored looser controls that Nvidia claimed would ensure global dominance of US technology. (A Commerce Department spokesperson told NYT that Bessent has never confronted Lutnick over his handling of Megaspeed.)

Any companies found violating the rules could face a “range of consequences,” the Commerce Department said after reportedly bending to Bessent’s pressure campaign. Those include possibly facing new import restrictions, stricter license requirements, downgrading their status in the US export control regime, or other changes to their company’s or their base country’s entity-list designations.

New rule may not be aggressively enforced

Although the summary of the rule change said that “Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion” of the anti-diversion policy, it’s unclear how aggressively the Commerce Department might enforce the rule, NYT noted.

Bessent has publicly criticized Lutnick for failing to sanction Megaspeed, and NYT reported that ultimately, enforcement of the stricter rules—which Bessent helped draft—“would be up to the Commerce Department.”

“The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?” Bessent said on a CNBC appearance. “I think it’s important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that.”

There’s even a push to oust Lutnick over his position on chips, but The Guardian reported that Donald Trump confirmed he has no plans to replace the AI industry-friendly commerce secretary. On Monday, Trump told reporters that Lutnick was right to delay blacklisting Megaspeed, because “if you didn’t delay it… you could have a blow-up with China.”

At the press gaggle, Trump aligned with China in saying that there’s no evidence yet that Alice Huang was a spy. He also joined a band of prominent tech leaders calling for Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, saying that it wasn’t a “bad idea.”

“Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy,” Trump said. “She may not be a spy.”

However, US investigators have alleged that they found “Alice Huang used industry contacts and a series of shell companies to access 240,000 chips banned for export into China,” CBS News reported .

Trump thinks China won’t react to rule change

China is unlikely to welcome the new rules, as it has consistently accused the US of fabricating the spying claims to justify imposing additional chip restrictions.

However, a senior Trump official, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive policy matters, told the NYT that Trump “did not expect countermeasures from China in response.”

Trump will be in China for an economic summit this week, including a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The new curbs could potentially disrupt those talks, according to Hong Yuan, a researcher and secretary-general of the Center for American Military Studies at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. Hong told the People’s Daily that China will likely view the rule change as politically motivated.

“Before any judicial causality was established, Washington handed down a political conviction, substituting suspicion for proof, espionage for personal contact, and an industrial embargo for private conduct,” Hong said. “The issue is not the cause of tighter controls, but a political catalyst.”

The new policy could hurt the US, experts told the Chinese outlets. Analysts told the South China Morning Post that the policy could “accelerate Chinese companies’ shift to domestic AI chips.” Other experts told the People’s Daily—which is the official newspaper of the Chinese Communist Party—that “the cost of switching back to US platforms will rise” over time. If that happened, it could potentially lock in Chinese technology over America’s in “the world’s largest single consumer market for chips,” experts said.

Sun Chenghao, senior fellow at the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing, told the People’s Daily that “what US companies stand to lose could be customers and technological influence for years to come.”

EFF and 27 other human rights organizations called on the European Commission today to retract a dangerous proposal granting its border agency Frontex to request that national authorities issue takedown orders for social media content and giving it “trusted flagger” status under the Digital Services Act (DSA), the EU regulation governing online platforms and content moderation in the region. The extraordinarily improper proposal not only disregards the provisions of the DSA but also places a mechanism of enforcement overreach in the hands of a law enforcement agency that has failed to safeguard people against serious human rights violations at EU borders. Under the proposal , Frontex has the power to “monitor publicly accessible social media content, detect developments relevant to external border management, and support action against illegal online content linked to border-security risks.” Granting Frontex trusted flagger privileges on top of its existing mandate risks creating a powerful mechanism for over-enforcement, stifling the free expression of migrants, asylum seekers, and other marginalized groups. We warned the Commission of these risks in a letter . The DSA is supposed to make online platforms more accountable and protect users’ fundamental rights, not give the EU power to sic its border police on people for exercising their right to free expression. EFF and other rights organizations have for years sounded alarms about potential abuse under the DSA’s trusted flagger provision, which gives “Digital Services Coordinators” the ability to award entities—including law enforcement agencies—a privileged channel to alert online platforms about illegal content. We’ve taken the firm position that law enforcement cannot be trusted to properly flag illegal content. In July, we told the Commission that giving law enforcement trusted flagger status could undermine fundamental rights and said that police agencies like Frontex should not be made trusted flaggers. The EU proposal gives Frontex decision-making power over free expression that is not envisaged under the DSA. First, content removal orders can only be issued by relevant national authorities. The DSA does not foresee a role for entities like Frontex to request such orders. Second, trusted flaggers notify platforms of suspected illegal content—platforms must prioritize these notices and they have sole responsibility to decide to remove content. It’s not flaggers’ role to request removal orders from national authorities. Combining these powers blur enforcement and flagging functions, which the Commission’s own draft guidelines on trusted flaggers explicitly caution against. “The risk of Frontex utilizing its power as both a Trusted Flagger and authority that can demand removal orders, to surveil user-generated speech, and over-flag content under the guise of ‘border security risk’ is clear. This will likely result in platforms over-censoring content and chilling the speech of already marginalized groups, particularly those from migrant and asylum-seeking communities,” the letter says. We urge the Commission to rescind the proposal. It undermines the DSA, threatens fundamental rights of citizens and non-citizens, and is enforcement overreach that does not align with international human rights standards.

stories.body:
Beijing stops short of confirming specific agenda, but Trump says denuclearisation, Iran war, trade and Ukraine will be among topics

The meeting of Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen this week will cover topics of “groundbreaking significance” including “safeguarding world peace”, the Chinese foreign ministry has said.

The confirmation of Thursday’s trilateral talks, the first of their kind, will take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit and cement Xi’s status as a global power broker as he presides over events in the glittering southern tech hub of Shenzhen.

At the White House, Trump told reporters he would be speaking to his Chinese and Russian counterparts about denuclearisation, the war in Iran, economics, trade and “my favourite subject, Ukraine”. US officials had earlier indicated that Trump would not discuss Russia’s war in Ukraine during the trip.

Trump also said he may meet North Korea’s Kim Jong-un in what would be their first meeting of his second term. “We may meet with Kim Jong-un also,” Trump said. “So that will be good … we have a chance to accomplish a lot.”

Asked whether Kim would be there, Trump said that he “may come”. “I don’t know,” he said. “That’s up to president Xi.”

Many, including the UN secretary general, António Guterres, had hoped the trilateral talks would be used to discuss reductions in nuclear arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers.

In a call this week, China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, “agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearisation”, the US state department said.

China was the last of the three powers to confirm the trilateral meeting was happening, and its statement stopped short of confirming specific agenda items.

“[The leaders] will exchange views in-depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance,” said its foreign ministry spokesperson, Mao Ning. “Stronger communication among China, Russia and the United States, along ​with managing differences and stabilising relations, serves the interests of all three countries.”

The Kremlin said: “The significance and symbolism of this meeting are hard to overestimate.”

Separately, the Kremlin ‌spokesperson Dmitry Peskov reportedly said on Monday that Putin would meet Kim, too, ​were he to be invited. “Of course, if ‌he is at the APEC ​summit,” Interfax quoted Peskov as saying. Peskov made ⁠his comments as ​Putin met ​a ​delegation in ​the Kremlin ‌from North ​Korea’s ​ruling Workers party.

Guterres said that if the three leaders “really commit themselves to a meaningful denuclearisation, it will be a great achievement for the world”. However, many analysts have warned to temper expectations of a major breakthrough.

Xi will “bask in the glow of China serving as the convener and agenda-setter”, wrote Brookings’ Ryan Hass in one such take. However, “symbolism may prove more enduring than the substance of this meeting”.

The three leaders would be approaching the talks with very different priorities, Xiaoyu Pu from the University of Nevada told the Guardian.

after newsletter promotion

China has rebuffed previous attempts to become embroiled in nuclear arms talks with ​Russia and the US, which ‌have the larger stockpiles. Trump, though, has said he wants to talk about denuclearisation, as well as the US-Israeli war in Iran. China, a top economic partner of Tehran, has sought to mediate in the conflict and says avoiding a return to hostilities is a “top priority”.

Trump’s remarks that he wanted to discuss Ukraine could stoke fears voiced by the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, that the trilateral talks could turn into a “Yalta 2, 3, 4 with a redistribution of influence”. Zelenskyy was referring to the 1945 pact between the US, UK and Soviet Union that created spheres of influence in Europe after the second world war.

“Ukraine-Russia is losing 25,000 soldiers a month, so we’ll be talking about that,” Trump said. He also deflected criticism of Putin in his remarks, saying the Kremlin leader could be “a lot tougher” in Ukraine and that he was already “backing down”.

US officials had said Trump was not expected to raise the issue, and the German president, Frank-Walter Steinmeier, said Xi showed “irritation” in a recent meeting when the idea of the trilateral talks covering Ukraine came up.

For Xi, much of the political benefit will be simply in “the ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table”, Peter Alexander, the Shanghai-based managing director at Z-Ben Advisors, told CNBC .

The Wall Street Journal reported last week that the Trump administration had pushed back against Beijing’s demands that the summit be tightly scripted, with prepared statements and not much room for discussion.

Sari Arho Havrén, of the Royal United Services Institute thinktank, wrote on X : “China dislikes surprises and wants to ensure neither Trump nor Putin steals the limelight from the host. Moreover, Xi doesn’t want to be dragged into a discussion about Ukraine or anything else he is not prepared for.”

stories.title: The young people caught up in Britain's Neets crisis
stories.summary: BBC News speaks to four of the million young people aged 16 to 24 who are not in work, education or training.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 17 November 2026, 00:06 GMT

The number of young people who are not in work, at school or in college is both an economic and moral crisis, a landmark report into the problem says.

The 241-page report, by ex-Labour minister Alan Milburn, has set out a raft of recommendations for the government to consider.

Ahead of its publication, four young people who are not in education, employment or training - those dubbed as "Neets" - told us why they can't get a job and how the government could help them get one.

Major report proposes welfare changes, apprenticeships and tax cuts to help 440,000 young people into work

Michael: 'Everything is experience, experience, experience'

We meet Michael after his early work experience shift at a supermarket

Michael, 19, who lives with his dad in the Wirral, says he dropped out of college and spent a year at home after his social anxiety "got really bad". It is "very easy" to fall out of the system, he says, if there is little support available.

Michael's story is not unique. There has been a large rise in anxiety and mental health problems in young people .

About one in five Neets have a mental health condition, according to 2025 data , external from the Department for Education (DfE) - more than double the rate in 2012.

Having signed up for Universal Credit, Michael was put in touch with the Merseyside Youth Association to help him find a job. He says mentors there have helped him improve his mental health, which led to him dropping out of college during his A-levels. He says that left him trapped inside his bedroom.

He says jobs in his area are scarce and those that do come up tend to go to older people with more experience. Michael says he is trapped in the cycle of not having the experience needed to build more.

"Everything is experience, experience, experience - that's the one thing that I always used to hear when going for jobs on my own without the help," he says.

We followed Michael for a day, meeting him after his 05:00 start for a work experience shift at a local supermarket that the Merseyside Youth Association helped him get.

Michael says getting his dog Dave motivated him to get out of the house and speak to people more

Lots of Neets receive Universal Credit. For under-25s, the standard rate is £338.58 a month , external , which Michael gets. For some people who cannot work because of a health condition, disability or long-term illness, an additional £217.26 to £429.80 per month may be available.

Ahead of the publication of his full review, it was reported that Milburn would recommend young people should no longer be able to claim those additional health-related benefits, as part of a major overhaul of the welfare system .

Michael acknowledges some young people may be "taking advantage" of the benefits system, but says most "just want the money to get by so they can get a job".

More recently, he has been doing shifts at the Merseyside Youth Centre's on-site cafe to gain more much-needed experience. His hope is to be in a steady job earning money this time next year, with space to have his own art studio one day.

"From three months ago I'm a different person," he says. "I can do stuff, keep going."

Maariyah: 'I send 20 job applications a week'

University graduate Maariyah says she is getting turned away from voluntary opportunities

Maariyah, a 22-year-old history and politics graduate, finished her university course last summer. Her dream is to work in museums.

However, she is currently unemployed and looking for any paid job after working a temporary six-month contract for a housing association earlier this year.

She says she spends hours each day in her local library - where she feels more able to focus than she can at home - submitting at least 20 tailored job applications a week.

Those who have not achieved GCSE-level qualifications are more likely to remain Neet for longer periods - however, an estimated one in 10 Neets are university graduates .

Maariyah says she is applying for roles in retail and restaurants, alongside unpaid work experience opportunities in the heritage sector.

But she says she has also been rejected for voluntary roles because they had too many applicants, or because she does not have enough experience. "I'm actively going out of my way to do unpaid work, only to get rejected from these positions," she says.

Not hearing back from employers "happens so often now that's it's like second nature", she says, adding that she finds it frustrating that many of her applications are likely to be screened by AI before a real person sees them.

Maariyah says she tailors her CV and cover letter for over 20 job applications a week

On the day we meet, Maariyah heads to the job centre for her Universal Credit appointment after a library job application session. She says she has noticed an improvement in the support she gets there since she first received the benefit in 2025.

This time, she will be getting some mandatory hospitality training, which she says she is "really glad" to have.

She feels there is a growing sense of disillusionment among others her age. Being on benefits has become normalised because it is so hard to find a job, she adds.

It makes her feel that going to a good university, getting certain grades and doing extracurricular activities "doesn't make a difference in the end".

"I would like employers to give young people a chance to gain experience and take a chance on hard-working people who at the end of the day want a job so that they can contribute to our economy and contribute to their own lives."

Matthieu: 'You might be surprised what people can do'

Matthieu has had many voluntary opportunities, but wants to find paid work

Matthieu, 19, from Edgware in north-west London, is autistic and currently volunteers at a gardening club and a computer repair shop.

We meet him in Finsbury Park, where he is helping to mulch some newly planted trees. Working in nature is calming, he says.

He is looking for work with the support of the charity Ambitious About Autism and his mentor, Annie. He previously did a year-long supported internship with the Whittington hospital.

Matthieu says speaking to people face-to-face there helped his confidence and he enjoyed being part of the team. At his family home, Matthieu's mentor Annie tells us that not having maths and English GCSE qualifications is a barrier to finding employment.

Matthieu says he's more of a manual worker and wants to work in a factory, warehouse or doing deliveries, so that he can contribute financially for his family.

Matthieu enjoys volunteering outside in nature

Those with learning difficulties or autism make up an estimated 12% of Neets, DfE data , external shows. Milburn's interim report , external , which was published in the summer, said 45% of Neets reported having a disability. He said the situation for young disabled people was "devastating".

To make work accessible to him, Matthieu says he would need an employer to take their time with him. He says: "I don't learn that quickly." But he thinks it would be worth it.

"Honestly, you might be surprised what the people can do when you take the time with them and give them that chance," Matthieu says.

Many employers say they can not afford to do so following rises to National Insurance contributions and the minimum wage , which is increasing further as part of announcements made in October's Budget.

Some businesses have told the BBC they are struggling to provide new jobs for young people due to these changes, as well as other factors like rising energy bills.

Although finding work is hard, Matthieu says he remains hopeful because of the support from his internship and job coach.

Alex: 'Places don't want to hire us'

Alex says there aren't many job opportunities in her area

Alex, 20, from St Helens, has been looking for work for a year. She struggles with anxiety and is looking for roles as a cleaner or in retail. She also shares caring responsibilities for her mum with her other family members.

We meet her at Spear, an employment and mindset coaching programme. Alex says her dream is to work with animals. She says she had been studying Level 3 animal management at college before dropping out last year because of her mental health.

"I was so burnt out," she says. "I was struggling to get out of bed, I couldn't do anything. I was dragging myself to college. I was like, 'No, I need to have a break for a bit and try and figure out what to do after that'."

Building up her resilience is something she now works on with a mentor, as well as job applications.

Alex says she is applying for "anything and everything" and wants to get off benefits. She is also currently receiving Universal Credit, which she says is "all the money that I've got until I get a job and I'm earning more".

Alex and her mentor, Grace, work on her CV during one-to-one sessions

When asked what she thinks about potential benefits cuts for young people out of work, Alex says not being able to access benefits would "make life so much worse".

And she says trying to find work in a place like St Helens is harder, because many businesses in the town centre have either "gone or moved or shut down".

"Lots of people think, 'well, young people just don't want to work,'" she says. "But we do. We so desperately want to work. Places don't want to hire us."

Milburn has already said the system isn't working for everyone, and that serious action is needed to avoid young Neets becoming a "lost generation".

Additional reporting by Branwen Jeffreys and Kate McGough

stories.title: EFF’s AI Cybersecurity Policy Framework
stories.summary: The news has been filled with stories recently of AI breaching the security of websites. And while it may feel like a new problem because of AI’s involvement, it turns out that there are longstanding existing cybersecurity safety best practices that these companies—some of the largest tech companies in the world—could and should have taken to prevent these breaches. Recent cybersecurity incidents have shown that some of the world’s largest tech companies have failed to take basic security precautions when testing frontier AI systems on internet-connected systems. Unfortunately, these failures resulted in breaches of numerous third-party websites, including an AI research-sharing platform called Hugging Face and the Australian healthcare system’s website. Even worse, AI developers failed to detect most of the incidents until long after they occurred due to inadequate monitoring of the AI systems during testing. Had the companies abided by basic, common sense security protocols, these incidents likely would not have occurred. While the White House and leaders of major AI companies have claimed that no action is necessary, understandably, lawmakers at all levels and of both parties are proposing legislation to create new, additional safety protocols. These incidents may warrant legislative action. However, the good news is that post-incident reports indicate new protocols are largely unnecessary. Following existing best practices would have been enough to prevent the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident and others like it. In other words, responsible AI developers can take immediate action to protect the public by implementing well-established security precautions as they develop and test their systems. Lawmakers should start by referencing existing legal protections, including claims like negligence, gross negligence, trespass to chattels, Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), and computer trespass statutes like the Consumer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) and analogous state law provisions, such as Section 502 of the California Penal Code. stories.title: Keepsake County review – eccentric stealing simulator with a social conscience
stories.summary: PC; Forward Instinct This irreverent stealth game depicts Samuel’s lonely life robbing garish, midwestern abodes – it’s a Shameless way to make a living For many people, McMansions are an eyesore, but for the protagonist of Keepsake County, a renowned burglar, they are an enticing opportunity. Prowling at purple-hued dusk, this unfussy thief is just as likely to steal a half-eaten slice of pizza or a naff ceramic ornament as he is an expensive set of golf clubs. It’s a sad, desperate way to make a living, a sense compounded by what this fledgling kleptomaniac carries his loot away in: a plastic shopping bag. Countless works have taken us to breadline America, from classic novel East of Eden to acclaimed TV crime drama Mare of Easttown. But Keepsake County is no prestige examination of the economic underbelly of the US. Rather, it is a stealing simulator with eccentric Adult Swim-style art and a darkly absurdist sense of humour that is expressed in its moment-to-moment action. For example, when I set off the alarm at a glinting modernist abode, I had to quickly dodge the gunshot fired my way by its maniacal owner, and as I scarpered across the surrounding grassy verge, I grabbed underpants off the clothesline just to make the long drive through the night worth it. I was reminded of Shameless (the US version) as much as Steinbeck. Continue reading...

stories.title: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
stories.summary: The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). Grand Theft Auto is now made by a huge team of nearly 5,000 people around the world but its central nervous system is still in Holyrood, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat. The setting of the latest Grand Theft Auto game really could not be further from the Scottish capital. Grand Theft Auto VI takes us to Vice City in the state of Leonida, a parody of Miami, Florida. It is a neon-soaked metropolis of sleaze and struggle, hard-partying excess juxtaposed with a barely concealed criminal underworld and unpredictable Florida madness. Continue reading...

stories.body:
Closing post

Time to recap

US President Donald Trump has said he “wouldn’t mind” seeing Jensen Huang reinstated as chief executive of Nvidia .

Speaking just days after Huang resigned after admitting cheating on his wife – and facing claims of an affair with a Chinese spy – Trump said Nvidia’s CEO had learned a lesson.

Trump told reporters:

double quotation mark “I think he learned a big lesson. I guess maybe one lesson is more important than ⁠another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that. “He could return. There’s a big group of ‌people that would like him to return,”

That group includes a collection of tech bosses including Elon Musk , Tim Sweeney , the founder and CEO of the video game publisher Epic Games, and Garry Tan , the president of business incubator Y Combinator. They all signed a letter calling on Nvidia to reinstate Huang.

Trump also suggested that Alice Huang, the first person reported to have had an affair with Jensen Huag, might not be a Chinese spy, as has been alleged.

He told reporters:

double quotation mark “Usually, what happens with that is that ​any woman ‌coming to the country ​that’s a ​beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy. I don’t know that she was a spy at all.”

Trump also insisted he isn’t planning to replace commerce secretary Howard Lutnick,

In a busy day for AI news, the US also issued a rule that will further restrict China’s access to the best AI chips from companies like Nvidia .

A new rule will force require data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil to obtain a US government license to purchase advanced AI chips from Nvidia and other American manufacturers.

Technology stocks have dropped again on Wall Street, as concern grows that the AI trade may be unravelling.

A senior policymaker at the European Central Bank warned there are growing risks from an “abrupt repricing” in markets and big losses if investor sentiment about artificial intelligence sours.

ECB’s vice president Boris Vujcic said the “rapid expansion of AI is creating new challenges for financial stability” in the 21-nation eurozone.

Nvidia’s shares have turned south again – they’re now down 2% at $159.74.

Other tech stocks are weakening too, pulling the Nasdaq Composite down by 2%.

Trump: Won't replace Lutnick

Donald Trump was also asked by reporters if he would replace commerce secretary Howard Lutnick, and replied: “No”.

Lutnick has come under pressure ever since US treasury secretary Scott Bessent blamed the commerce department for the fact the US had not imposed export restrictions on certain Nvidia chips to China.

But Trump backed Lutnick , telling reporters that the commerce secretary “might have delayed” putting Megaspeed on the US trade blacklist, but then suggested that “he was doing that because if you didn’t delay it . . . you could have a blow-up with China”.

Nvidia’s shares are shaking off their early drop, as investors hear Trump’s supportive words for Jensen Huang.

They’re now down just 0.55% at $161.95.

Trump: Wouldn't mind Huang being reinstated as Nvidia CEO

Newsflash: US President ⁠Donald ⁠Trump has declared that he ⁠would ​not ‌mind ‌seeing Jensen ‌Huang reinstated as the chief executive ‌officer of ​Nvidia.

Trump is speaking to reporters now, ahead of his trip to Manila to attend the ASEAN summit.

The president added that the suggestion that Huang could return to Nvidia is not a bad idea. He says the ex-CEO has learned a lesson, and denies that national security has been put at risk.

UPDATE: Trump said:

double quotation mark “I think having Jensen go back – a lot of people are asking Jensen – they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea.”

That’s quite an intervention, as an open letter circulates calling for the chip giant to reinstate Huang.

Trump also said that he doesn’t know that the woman involved with Huang – Alice Huang – was a Chinese spy.

Update: he said:

double quotation mark “Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy. She may not be a spy.”

[Reminder: the New York Times reported last week that secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington in spring this year, warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy]

Nvidia shares drop by 2.67%

Newsflash: Nvidia’s shares have dropped by 2.67% at the start of trading.

They’ve dropped to $158.51 each. That knocks around $100bn off Nvidia’s market capitalisation, lowering it to $3.82trn.

That’s down from $4.5tn a little over a week ago, before news broke that Jensen Huang had conducted an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

Investors have a lot to digest, from the push to have Jensen Huang reinstalled as Nvidia’s CEO ( see here ) to the new US clampdown on remote access to AI chips ( see here ).

There may also be jitters ahead of Nvidia’s financial results, scheduled for tomorrow afternoon.

Tom Stevenson, investment director at Fidelity International, explains:

double quotation mark “This is the anxious backdrop to a week of potentially market-moving events that include the latest figures from Nvidia, the publication of minutes from the latest Fed meeting, and the widely anticipated IPO of Anthropic, the business behind the Claude AI model. “Nvidia’s results are always closely scrutinised. But never more so than in the week after its founder CEO stepped down. The numbers will be good again, with revenues of $108bn pencilled in, 12% more than in the prior quarter. But the attention will be elsewhere, on the future direction of the company under new leadership.

SFO charges eight people over collapse of London Capital & Finance

Newsflash: The UK’s Serious Fraud Office (SFO) has charged eight individuals in connection with its investigation into the collapse of London Capital & Finance Plc (LCF), one of Britain’s biggest retail investment scandals.

The SFO says that Michael Andrew Thomson (53), Simon Hume-Kendall (73), Elten Barker (53), Paul Careless (51), Robert Sedgwick (78) and John Russell-Murphy (52) have each been charged with conspiracy to defraud. Helen Hume-Kendall (64) has been charged with concealing criminal property.

An eighth defendant has been charged with conspiracy to defraud and acting in contravention of a director disqualification undertaking.

The collapse of LCF, which promised high interest rates on “mini-bonds” between 2013 and 2018, cost about 11,600 investors more than £237m, leaving taxpayers to pay a £120m compensation bill.

US announces new rules to limit remote ccess to advanced AI chips

Newsflash: The US Commerce Department has issued a new rule to limit remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips by certain third countries.

The interim final rule (IFR) is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries, the US government says.

The IFR will require licenses to reexport advanced AI chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil.

This move follows reports that Singapore-based Megaspeed , the company where suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang worked, had transferred advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies.

The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry & Security explains:

double quotation mark Rapid advancement in cloud computing and SI infrastructure have made it increasingly possible to access advanced American computing capabilities remotely, including through data centers located outside countries subject to U.S. export restrictions. This IFR addresses this evolving technological landscape by further aligning protections governing remote access to advanced computing capabilities with existing controls on the physical shipment of sensitive American technology.

Marketwatch’s Mark DeCambre has three questions for anyone considering taking up the CEO’s role at Nvidia:

What am I inheriting? What has the board learned about the export concerns and Nvidia’s financing deals? What’s still unresolved?

How much of the company do I actually get to run? Who‘ll be on the board a year from now, and will they back me if I change a strategy that Jensen put in place?

Who can I count on to stay at Nvidia? If Jensen goes to work for a competitor, which of the people I need at Nvidia might take his call?

Insurance industry workers: how is climate-related risk managed in your company?

Whether you’re a modeller, actuary or underwriter, we’d like to hear how the insurance industry is dealing with climate risk – click here for more :

Tensions are building in the markets ahead of the stockmarket float of AI firm Anthropic.

Anthropic is due to launch its shares onto the stock market on Thursday. And having initially hoped for a $2tn valuation, it may come to market at a lower valuation of $1.5bn, or even less….

Trading platform IG are running an “Anthrophic IPO Market Cap” market where customers can take bets on the company’s valuation when it floats.

So far today, the contract is down 0.7% at around $1.359bn.

Chris Beauchamp, Chief Market Analyst at investing and trading platform IG , says:

double quotation mark “IG’s pre-IPO market continues to see interest from buyers, with the price finding a low around $1.4 trillion following last week’s volatility in tech. This represents a significant drop from the $2 trillion level seen at the end of October, but the less ambitious pricing seems preferable to a pricier offering that then struggles on day one. Sentiment is too fragile right now to weather a bad IPO for such a big name. Nvidia’s troubles do not augur well for the rest of the AI complex, making a strong debut for Anthropic more important than ever.”

stories.title: Nvidia dismisses 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign as Trump backs effort to reinstate ex boss
stories.summary: A number of tech figures have backed an effort asking the AI chip giant to give Jensen Huang his job back.
