stories.title: At a glance: Key proposals from Milburn's Neets report
stories.summary: A major review proposes widespread changes to help get young people into work across the UK.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The review has proposed widespread changes to tax, welfare, and education

Published 1 hour ago

A major review by former minister Alan Milburn has proposed widespread changes to help get young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) into work across the UK.

His report - which has now been published in full , external - says the UK should aim to reduce the rate of Neet young people from 13% to about 5% by 2036.

Its proposals relate mostly to England, with a recommendation that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland adapt the principles to suit their own systems.

Here is a summary of the key points from the review:

Major report proposes welfare changes, apprenticeships and tax cuts to help 440,000 young people into work

Rights for young people

Young people should have a legal right to a route into education, training or work, and would be supported to do so under an "opportunity guarantee"

A new, locally-led Youth Opportunity Service in England would give young people one named advisor and a personalised participation plan - spelling out what action needs to be taken, by whom, and when

Tax, spending and other policy decisions should be put through a "youth opportunity test", to ensure they consider impact on younger generations

Schools

Prevention should start early, with primary and secondary schools required to identify and support pupils at risk of becoming Neet

Schools would also be required to offer work experience

A new performance measure would assess schools based on where their pupils end up

A new writing, numeracy and oracy check for pupils in Key Stage 3 (Years 7 to 9)

Colleges and apprenticeships

An extra 150,000 18- to 24-year-olds studying further education courses at colleges and other training providers each year

College funding to be based on how students perform and where they end up, rather than on how many students there are

A new digital open college, part-funded by employers and private investors, which would allow young people to study courses from colleges and universities

Aim to double the number of young people completing apprenticeships over the next decade - with more than a third of young people starting one every year

Where has the most jobs for 18-24 year-olds? Use our look-up to find out Published 45 minutes ago

Watch: What's in the Milburn review? Published 1 hour ago

The young people caught up in Britain's Neets crisis Published 1 hour ago

Employers

An extra 170,000 job and apprenticeship opportunities to be created through employer incentives

Employers who take on any young person who has been Neet for six months should receive a £3,000 payment

Small businesses - with fewer than 50 employees - which do so should receive an extra £2,000

There would be an extra £2,000 payment if the young person has been in care or is disabled

Lower National Insurance costs for 21- to 24-year-olds, starting in retail and hospitality

Large employers should tell job applicants when they are unsuccessful

Mental health

Young people who are already Neet should have guaranteed access to fast-track services like talking therapies and counselling within three months

These should be accessible without a diagnosis

A new digital-first mental health care service should be the "starting point for young people to access help"

The government should introduce national maximum waiting times for young people's mental health care from 2028

Fitness to work, or "fit notes", to be issued through the new Youth Opportunity Service, rather than GPs

Welfare

An "entirely new benefits system" for under-25s

Young people to no longer get the health top-up of Universal Credit, which provides extra money for people whose health conditions limit their capacity to work

They would also no longer receive Personal Independence Payments (Pip), which help with the extra living costs of having a long-term health condition or disability

Instead, a new youth allowance would be set at the basic rate of Universal Credit for under-25s, with a higher rate for those living independently

A "local flexible health and disability fund" to be run by the local Youth Opportunity Service would pay for extra costs while a young person is receiving support

stories.body:
Some firms are directing refunds to corporate leadership instead of reimbursing consumers, ProPublica finds

Several companies that received refunds for paying Donald Trump ’s tariffs have put those funds towards corporate bonuses instead of reimbursing consumers, an investigation from ProPublica has found.

After analyzing securities filings and earnings calls, ProPublica identified at least nine companies who said they are receiving tariff refunds and noted they are directing some of those funds to their leadership.

Stanley Black & Decker, a tool company that makes common household products including vacuums, electric drills and measuring tapes, told its consumers they were forced to raise prices because of Trump’s import fees, ProPublica reported. The company is expected to receive at least $298m in tariff reimbursements and indicated some of it will go to bonuses. Executives at TJ Maxx and Marshalls, discount department stores that are set to receive tariff refunds, also said the same.

A spokesperson for TJ Maxx and Marshalls, which are owned by the same TJX parent company, confirmed ProPublica’s reporting, and said that the company received an aggregate of $331m in refunds for a portion of the tariffs covered in the supreme court ruling. Because of these refunds, the company now has “accrue incremental expenses of $112 million for year-end incentive compensation and discretionary bonuses for eligible associates globally”, the spokesperson said.

“Given that this is an accrual, and we have not reached the end of our current fiscal year, we have not disclosed any breakout beyond this,” the company spokesperson said.

In financial disclosures, Stanley Black & Decker said the refund it received “was partially offset by directly attributable costs for variable incentive compensation”, according to ProPublica. Stanley Black & Decker did not immediately respond to request for comment.

The Trump administration has refunded at least $100bn to companies since August, about 60% of roughly $131bn in tariffs, after the supreme court ruled that Trump’s “liberation day” tariffs were illegal. The court ruled that the tariffs were unlawful because they overstepped his executive authority and should have required congressional approval.

Some companies immediately sued the US government for refunds after the ruling, though Trump signaled that he would “remember” which companies requested reimbursements and praised companies for holding off. The Trump administration has not specified which companies are receiving refunds, despite requests for information, according to ProPublica.

Though many companies said publicly that they had to increase prices because of tariffs, it has largely been unclear what companies are doing with their tariff refunds.

In its analysis, ProPublica found that almost all the companies that have publicly said they plan to use their tariff reimbursements to refund customers are those that deal directly with other businesses, rather than directly consumers. Some companies have remained “vague” about their plans for the reimbursements and have not specified whether those funds will go towards price decreases or holding back on future increases, according to the report.

after newsletter promotion

Research has shown that US consumers have shouldered some of the cost of tariffs, with the New York Federal Reserve estimating that 26% of tariff increases pass through to consumer prices. The Yale Budget Lab estimated that tariffs cost households about $900 annually under current laws.

Tariffs are one of several of Trump’s economic policies that have proven unpopular with voters, reflected in the widespread victories Democrats notched in the November midterms. A year after Trump’s tariffs were announced, a survey from the Pew Research Center found that 63% of Americans felt little or no confidence in his handling of tariffs.

Republican candidates across the country were largely punished for Trump’s tariffs and other White House decisions that have led to greater inflation. In the Associated Press’s survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters, two-thirds said that Trump’s decisions had fueled inflation, about half of the number of 2022 midterm voters who said the same thing about former president Joe Biden.

stories.body:
Experts say US president may lean toward global affairs after domestic influence curtailed in midterm elections

Donald Trump is embarking on his first overseas trip since his Republican party’s thumping midterm repudiation by US voters, in what may herald a renewed focus on foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency.

The US president will meet his Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, for their first trilateral summit, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. Before that, he will land in Manila in the Philippines on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit.

At the Asean summit, Trump is expected to sign a trade agreement with Thailand , push deals with other countries and lobby fellow leaders to favour the US over China on artificial intelligence.

He will also take part in the first leaders’ meeting of the Quad partnership – consisting of the US, Japan, India and Australia – since he returned to the White House in January 2025.

White House officials said the president would be accompanied to Apec by Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX entrepreneur who spent almost $500m (£380m) unsuccessfully supporting Republican candidates in this month’s midterms. The reason for Musk’s presence has not been explained.

The China leg of the trip will take place amid the continuing fallout from the Nvidia spying scandal , which prompted the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, to resign amid revelations he had had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Trump is under pressure to raise the matter with Xi when they hold a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of Apec.

The US president has said he does not plan to bring up the subject ; administration officials insist he will not do so and that the meeting will be dedicated to implementing a trade agreement between the two superpowers.

Huang persuaded the Trump administration to lift restrictions on the sale of Nvidia’s AI chips to China that had been imposed during Joe Biden’s presidency.

Mao Ning, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson, told reporters on Monday that at the trilateral summit, Xi, Trump and Putin “will exchange views in depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance”.

Some analysts have characterised the meeting as a “big three” gathering echoing the 1945 Yalta meeting of Winston Churchill, Franklin D Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin that in effect carved up postwar Europe, between a communist-ruled east and a democratic, capitalist west.

Such a prospect has alarmed Ukraine , which fears that Putin – who initially suggested the trilateral meeting – will use it to persuade Trump and Xi to agree to a settlement of the war with Russia on Moscow’s terms.

However, Trump has said Ukraine will not be up for debate at the meeting and that its main purpose will be to discuss ending the US’s war with Iran and “denuclearisation” – shorthand for a deal among the three powers to limit nuclear arms.

That is believed to be unpalatable to China , which has been increasing its nuclear arsenal, and has signalled an unwillingness to enter into reduction agreements until it is closer to parity with the US and Russia.

after newsletter promotion

Analysts say the main beneficiary of the three-way meeting is likely to be Putin, whose standing will be boosted by being treated on an equal footing by two other leaders whose countries are, in reality, much more powerful.

Expectations of a substantial agreement are low.

Lyle Goldstein, an international affairs fellow and China specialist at Brown University in the US, said the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting would not have a substantive result. “There will be no ‘Yalta’, as many have feared,” he said.

Jonathan Czin, the Michael Armacost chair in foreign policy studies at the Brookings Institution, said Trump’s lame duck status would deter Xi and Putin from trying to reach long-term arrangements with the US.

“Both men know Trump’s time is expiring even more quickly than his leverage – and that he will be irrelevant in a mere 26 months [when his term expires],” Czin told an online Brookings forum . “Why would either man make a deal with a leader whose time and leverage are waning? They will only do it if they think they can pilfer more from Trump diplomatically than they will be able to gain from the next American president.”

Nevertheless, Goldstein – who took soundings on Chinese expectations for the summit in a visit to Shenzhen last week – predicted Trump would follow the pattern of previous presidents by turning increasingly to global affairs while he faces the prospect of his influence on the domestic front being curtailed after the Democrats’ victories in the House of Representatives and the Senate.

“The president has been badly damaged by the election and will have limited prospects for the next two years,” he said. “That may cause him to be more active in foreign policy since he can act in that domain with fewer constraints. It would not surprise me if Trump is ready to go all-out to make some further splash in foreign policy.”

With the risks of reigniting the war with Iran high and the Russia-Ukraine war still resistant to a diplomatic resolution despite White House efforts, Goldstein suggested Trump could attempt “a dramatic foreign policy flourish in Asia”, such as an agreement with Kim Jong-un, the North Korean dictator with whom he has frequently boasted of having a close relationship. Kim is not expected to attend the Apec gathering, although there have been rumours he may appear.

stories.title: Failed asylum seekers face removal without five-day notice period
stories.summary: Under proposed new rules, the Home Office would have six months in which to remove a person without telling them in advance.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 17 November 2026, 01:24 GMT

The government is to change the law so that it no longer has to give failed asylum seekers notice before they are removed from the country.

Currently, people are given five working days' notice but ministers believe this leads to last-minute appeals which delay the process.

Under the new rules, once an asylum claim fails, the Home Office would have six months in which to remove the applicant without telling them in advance.

The move was criticised by the Refugee Council which said: "Removing people at such short notice will cause unnecessary distress and anxiety to people."

Imran Hussain, the director of the refugee charity, said: "The reality is that voluntary removals are far more effective at removing people than enforced returns.

"If you assist people to return with dignity, many will take that option, at far lower cost to the taxpayer."

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood will make the change by amending the Immigration and Asylum Bill which is currently going through Parliament.

The amendment will scrap the notice requirement for those who have exhausted the asylum appeals process.

Instead, the Home Office will have the power to remove people immediately, a power that will remain in place for up to six months.

The Home Office has not said how many additional people it thinks it will be able to remove but has pointed to Denmark where the number of migrants awaiting removal more than halved over five years to under 1,000 after a similar policy was introduced.

The previous government, led by Sir Keir Starmer, had pledged to clear the asylum backlog.

An asylum seeker is someone who wants to be in the UK because they say they cannot live safely in their own country due to persecution or violence.

The government must house an asylum seeker if they cannot financially support themselves while their claim is being considered. There were 89,089 people in asylum accommodation as of June 2026.

About 18% of those people, 16,021, were in hotels. These are used when there is not enough shared housing available, such as houses of multiple occupation (HMOs) or former military sites .

The government has pledged to stop the use of hotels by 2029.

More people are in hotels across the south of England than elsewhere in the UK, while HMOs are more common in the north of England and Scotland.

A modern browser with JavaScript and a stable internet connection is required to view this interactive

Type in a postcode or the name of a local council below to see how many asylum seekers are housed in the area

A total of 85,891 people applied for asylum in the UK from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 21% on the same period in the previous year.

Most people who arrive in the UK by small boat claim asylum, but they were only 40% of all asylum seekers from July 2025 to June 2026.

The rest include people who arrived by other illegal means or who came to the UK legally and applied for asylum while holding, or just after holding, a valid visa.

It can take years for the government to decide whether someone should be granted asylum.

In June 2026, 40,168 people - across 32,401 asylum applications - were waiting for an initial decision. The number of people awaiting an initial decision was down by 56% on the previous year.

As of June 2026, a further 90,341 refused asylum applications were part of a second backlog, waiting the outcome of an appeal in the courts. This was up by 51% on the previous year.

Together, these initial decision and appeal cases form the government’s total asylum applications backlog, which it has pledged to clear .

Refugee status was granted in about 38% of asylum decisions made by the Home Office from July 2025 to June 2026.

About 39% of asylum appeal cases concluded between January 2026 to December 2026 resulted in a previous refusal decision being overturned.

In June 2026, there were 40,168 people waiting for an initial decision on asylum application claims and a further 90,341 waiting for the outcome of an appeal in the courts.

Between July 2025 and June 2026, 38% of asylum decisions led to the applicant being granted refugee status.

Forty percent of all asylum claims come from people who arrived in the UK by small boat.

The remaining 60% of claims are made by people who arrived in the country by other illegal means or who came to the UK legally and subsequently applied for asylum.

Anna Turley, minister for border security and asylum, said: "We are ensuring those migrants who have exhausted their right to appeal can be removed promptly, rather than being given an opportunity to frustrate their legitimate removal from this country.

"This bill will restore order and control to the system, ensuring it is swift and fair."

'It felt like I was dying’: Why some teenagers don’t go to school

Published 16 November 2026

The stories of Eva and Mali - which you can watch in the video above - and the many teenagers like them who don't go to school, either regularly or at all, strike to the heart of one of the many big challenges the Milburn Review is seeking to address.

The government-commissioned work, led by former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, is looking into how to solve the problem of nearly one million young people not being in employment, education or training, or Neet.

A key challenge is addressing the issue of school absence.

The government believes around a third of young people who are persistently absent in Years 10 and 11 in England go on to be Neet, compared with 10% of those who are not persistently absent.

Persistent absence almost doubles between Years 7 and 9, reaching around one in four children by Year 9.

Eva, 13, stopped going to school after struggling with the transition to secondary school

Thirteen-year-old Eva hadn't been to school for 15 months before September.

She described how she used to get up every morning, try to get ready for school and get stuck by the front door.

Mali, 18, stopped attending school three years ago when she was in year 10.

We shared their stories with the decision makers and those who want to be our decision makers – in other words, those in government and those who would like to be.

It offers an insight into the political arguments to come.

Labour reckons the Conservatives' education reforms of the last decade and a half served academic high achievers very well but created what one source described as an an "endless treadmill of failure" for some - and so let them down.

A government spokesperson said: "When children feel they belong at school, they show up, and when they show up, they achieve."

Therefore, the spokesperson added, "the education secretary is driving ambitious reforms to boost attendance" and "intervene earlier when children need support".

The Liberal Democrats also sought to pin the blame on the Tories.

Munira Wilson, who speaks for the party on education, said "the Conservatives failed to give them the support they needed after lockdown, and years of underinvestment in their recovery are now showing up in rising mental health figures". She added that "every young person should feel they belong".

These reactions prompt some of the big questions that arise from Eva and Mali's experiences.

Where should responsibility for their situations lie? The individual, the parents, the rules in the pandemic, schools, colleges, mental health provision?

Perhaps a combination of all of these things in some instances and other things besides.

The Conservatives have pushed back strongly against the criticism from Labour and the Liberal Democrats.

Shadow education secretary Laura Trott told the BBC: "We mustn't give up on any child, every day a child misses school sets them back.

"Schools are doing great work to bring absence down. Those children who have special education needs or are struggling to leave home, need specialist support and in some cases specialist schools."

And she added: "High academic standards lift everyone up. It is insulting to suggest that not all children are capable of good academic outcomes. Too much maths and English are not making young people Neet."

Former Conservative cabinet minister Suella Braverman, now Reform UK's education spokesperson, told us: "As someone who co-founded and chaired an outstanding state school with a high proportion of children on free school meals but a below average school absence rate, it is clear that the culture and teaching in a school can make a huge difference."

She added that "greater parental engagement" and a "culture of perseverance" were essential too.

The government is expected to accept the broad thrust of Alan Milburn's report, before responding in detail in the next month or so.

We are told there will be an announcement from Education Secretary Lucy Powell directly relevant to Eva, Mali and the many like them, later this week.

stories.title: Five EU countries announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda
stories.summary: Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands have announced a "return hub" for failed asylum seekers.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 16 November 2026

Five EU countries will open a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda next year as part of a broader push to boost removals.

Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to open a "return hub" ready to accept transfers in 2027, the Dutch and Danish governments announced in statements.

The countries said the scheme would apply to migrants staying illegally in their nations who are subject to deportation, with the Dutch government adding it will provide an alternative if deportees cannot be returned to their country of origin.

Deportees will be able to either integrate into Rwandan society or return to their home country, the nations said.

The scheme will apply to people who have exhausted their legal avenues to stay in the five nations - unlike a scrapped British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed. Legal challenges meant the UK deal never took off, and it was eventually junked by the incoming Labour government in 2024 .

Downing Street has not ruled out the UK joining the scheme, saying they will watch it "with interest".

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said the plan to open a centre in Rwanda had no "future or humanity", according to AFP news agency.

"I don't see any future or humanity in that. It's not the solution," Sanchez told the Spanish broadcaster Telecinco, AFP reported.

The five countries say the plan to send migrants abroad is in line with EU and international law, but human rights bodies say it could violate migrant rights.

The deal follows a recent EU reform that allowed for the creation of hubs outside of the bloc.

In a joint press conference in Vienna on Monday, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said the five countries wanted to relieve European asylum systems and stop traffickers arranging deadly trips across the Mediterranean.

In a written statement, the Dutch government said the five countries will "only return single men" as part of the first phase of the deal, adding that the focus for the Netherlands "will be on persons from countries of origin in the same region as Rwanda".

Once in Rwanda, people will be able to integrate into society, which means they will have the right of residence, as well as access to education, healthcare, the labour market and the legal system.

Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said the country is commmited to working with European partners to provide a "safe, legal and dignified solution for migrants".

He added that they would also work on "correcting the global imbalance in economic opportunities", which he called a "key driver of irregular migration".

Ahead of the announcement, diplomatic sources told the AFP news agency the hub is expected to initially run as a pilot, hosting about 100 people, with each of the five nations possibly sending about 20 migrants.

The United Nations' International Organisation for Migration (IOM) could play an ancillary role.

"IOM has a long history of providing assistance to migrants in situations of transit, including in complex contexts," an IOM spokesperson said, adding the agency was in discussions with some EU countries "on plans for the establishment of return hubs or similar mechanisms".

With elections approaching in several EU nations, administrations have been under pressure to show they can control migration.

Concerns around security, struggling economies and disillusionment with governing parties have all had a major role in shaping attitudes towards people leaving their home countries .

Human Rights Watch's senior Africa researcher Clementine de Montjoye said the choice of Rwanda would be a cause of concern as it had a "well-established record of repression of dissent, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment in detention" and support for armed rebels in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo.

"Paying Kigali to host a deportation programme would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad."

The independent EU Agency for Fundamental Rights argued any third country hosting a return hub should "respect fundamental rights", including that people should not be sent to a country where they face serious risk of persecution.

The agency added that unaccompanied children should not be sent to a return hub, which the Dutch government has confirmed will not take place.

According to the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, there were almost 110,000 irregular border crossings into the EU in the first 10 months of 2026, which represents a 29% decrease compared to the previous year.

In October, about 18,100 crossings were detected, which is about 6% less than October 2025 but 22% more than in September "largely because of a sharp rise in arrivals on the Western African route to the Canary Islands".

Watch: 'Hard Brexit we were given not good enough for Britain,' says Burnham

Published 16 November 2026

The prime minister has argued the UK has lost more than it has gained from leaving the European Union in a speech ahead of a UK-EU summit later this week.

Speaking at the Lord Mayor's Banquet on Monday, Andy Burnham compared the UK's Brexit deal to the "emperor's new clothes" - saying "a needlessly hard Brexit" created barriers for businesses and the promise to "take back control" was not delivered.

He is due to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility with the bloc at Friday's summit, after the substance of those deals was set by his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

The Conservatives have said Labour are "dragging us into the European Union via the back door".

In his first major speech on foreign policy, the prime minister said that following the summit he would begin new discussions with the EU about options for "our long-term relationship".

However, he warned it would take time and insisted that "at every stage the British people will be the boss".

Burnham has ruled out major changes before the next general election.

On the UK's current relationship with EU, Burnham said: "It's like the emperor's new clothes – where no-one is prepared to say the obvious truth. Well, I say it as I see it. And to be frank, the emperor has nothing on.

"The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we have gained."

Ahead of Friday's UK-EU summit, Burnham set out three tests for any agreement.

Firstly, that it must be consistent with Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledge that there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement".

He also said it must improve the original Brexit deal and bring it closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016.

Finally, he said any deal must pass the "Makerfield test" of providing tangible improvements to people's everyday lives - a reference to voters in Burnham's Greater Manchester constituency.

He also said the prospect of a new deal is a "win-win" and illustrates a "new approach".

"Not adversarial. No longer burning bridges. But being constructive and positive - showing that we can come together to confront shared challenges."

Burnham said "Britain was back in the game in a big way" and would be a country that "leads with its values".

UK will have 'voice' but no vote on EU food rules in Brexit reset Published 21 hours ago

Burnham says 'win-win' deal can be agreed between UK and EU Published 4 days ago

Burnham's push for closer EU ties causes ripples in his party and others Published 5 days ago

This week's summit will see the UK seek to agree further changes to former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's deal, struck in May 2025, covering fishing, trade and other areas.

The UK and EU have agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports ahead of the meeting.

The government argues the agreement will help cut costs for businesses and could bring down prices for shoppers.

However, critics say the deal will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels, aligning with EU regulations without being able to vote on them.

Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated to EU nations.

These deals were close to being finalised under Sir Keir, with only some details still to be worked out.

New campaign against EU membership launches ahead of UK-EU summit Published 3 days ago

Brexit referendum 'possible' in Labour election manifesto, says Burnham Published 30 September

As a candidate in the Makerfield by-election that propelled his return to Parliament, Burnham had promised not to "re-run" Brexit arguments and said he was "not proposing that the UK considers rejoining the EU".

However, since becoming prime minister he has said he wants to explore a different long-term relationship with the bloc.

He has suggested potential options for the future could range from no changes to the UK-EU relationship, to rejoining the customs union, the single market or a fresh referendum on full EU membership.

The prime minister has stressed any changes would require a mandate from the public at a general election.

Boris Johnson, who was prime minister when the UK left the EU in 2020 and negotiated the original Brexit deal, has warned Burnham against "wasting his premiership" on Europe.

He told the Daily Telegraph , external he believed the public would back Brexit again if Burnham forced another vote on the issue.

"It is madness to escalate the Brexit issue as your political priority," Johnson told the paper.

"He will impale himself and his party on this point, and he needs to move off it because he won't win – because the reality is that people are not fools."

Deputy Conservative leader Alex Burghart accused Burnham of "reopening a debate the country settled long ago, while ignoring the challenges facing Britain today".

Reform UK has said one of the "key benefits" of Brexit is that Britain no longer has to "adhere to ridiculous EU rules", and argued that any form of alignment could have a negative impact on the country's trade policy.

The Liberal Democrats have said the draft deal on food exports is a "patch, not a fix" and that the "real solution is to re-join the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU".

The Green Party of England and Wales has called for the UK to re-join the customs union, with leader Zack Polanski previously saying "full membership of the EU remains the best option for the UK".

stories.title: UK budget leaves NI underfunded, O'Dowd says
stories.summary: Northern Ireland's public funding has worsened relative to rest of the UK as a result of the Westminster budget, Stormont's Finance Minister has claimed.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
John O'Dowd believes that public services will be underfunded by around £450m over the next three years

Published 16 November 2026

Northern Ireland's public funding has worsened relative to the rest of the UK as a result of the Westminster budget, Stormont's finance minister has claimed.

John O'Dowd said the Treasury's figures show that NI will now be funded below its objective "level of need" next year and the year after.

Needs-based funding recognises that it costs more to deliver public services in some parts of the UK compared to others.

The Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant has offered £1.5bn over the next three years and said if Stormont ministers accept this, that will take funding comfortably above the level of need.

O'Dowd said: "Treasury's own assessment shows that we are underfunded, relative to our current estimate of need, in 2027/28 and 2028/29.

"My officials' analysis also indicates that we are underfunded this year, and therefore in each year of the Spending Review."

It is understood O'Dowd believes that in cash terms this means public services will be underfunded by around £450m over the next three years.

It comes as executive ministers held further talks about the budget deadlock on Monday afternoon at Stormont Castle.

First and deputy first ministers react

Following the meeting, First Minister Michelle O'Neill said the Secretary of State is "not listening" to the Stormont executive over its continuing budget pressures.

She said their concerns may now need to be "elevated" to the prime minister and warned Andy Burnham that Stormont's political and financial stability were "two sides of the one coin".

She reiterated the executive's argument that Northern Ireland has been significantly "underfunded" in comparison to the devolved governments in Scotland and Wales.

O'Neill said it was "very clear that we have taken this to where we can with the Secretary of State".

Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly said what the executive was asking of the government was "absolutely reasonable".

Speaking after the executive meeting, she said it was "positive that we're continuing to discuss these issues".

"What we are asking the UK government to do is absolutely reasonable, and that is to work with us to try to get a balanced budget to actually fulfil the legal duties that we have," she said.

"We will be doing everything we can in the DUP to support getting that budget settlement to enable us to do public sector pay."

What is needs-based funding?

Needs-based funding attempts to give each part of the UK the same quality of public services.

It recognises that public services can be more expensive to deliver in NI because, for example, it has a more rural and dispersed population than in England.

NI is therefore assessed as needing £124 per head for every £100 per head spent on public services in England. This is known as the 124% needs-based funding level.

It is understood the Treasury figures and Department of Finance calculations show NI will be funded at around 123% this year and in the two following years.

How does this impact budget negotiations?

Stormont ministers are currently trying to get more money from the UK government which they say they need to reach a balanced budget.

The secretary of state has offered £1.5bn over the next three years.

Stormont ministers say that is not enough and O'Dowd says the needs-based underfunding makes the situation worse.

"Around one third of the currently proposed financial package from the British government is required on its own to merely bring us to the 124% level of need," he added.

What has the UK government said?

Chris Bryant said that if Stormont ministers accept his offer that will take funding comfortably above the level of need.

"The NI executive has been offered an additional £1.5bn over the next three years, which would mean NI remains funded above 126% in all years of the Spending Review," he said.

"If the executive is to avoid a major public services crisis in the new year it needs to set a budget as a matter of urgency. That is its legal responsibility."

stories.title: Miliband says he won't resign if government approves Rosebank oil field
stories.summary: Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh is to make a decision on Britain's largest untapped oil field.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 16 November 2026

Ed Miliband said he will "definitely not" resign if the government approves the Rosebank oil field, despite previously calling the scheme "climate vandalism".

The foreign secretary told the BBC he would "obey collective responsibility", which requires ministers to publicly support decisions made by the government even if they disagree with them.

A decision on the future of the oil field off Shetland will be taken by Miatta Fahnbulleh, who succeeded Miliband as energy secretary in July.

Some Labour MPs oppose the project, while the Conservatives argue there is a need to "get Britain drilling". Miliband publicly raised his concerns about Rosebank while Labour was in opposition.

Appearing on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Miliband was reminded that in 2023 he said the project would be a "colossal waste of taxpayer money and climate vandalism" , external .

Asked if it could be assumed he would resign if his successor decided to develop Rosebank, Miliband replied: "No, definitely not because I obey collective responsibility.

"Miatta Fahnbulleh will make the decision on this. As you know, it's what they call a quasi-judicial decision so she looks at all the evidence and then reaches a conclusion."

Miliband said he would not "second guess her decision" on Rosebank.

He added he supported the energy secretary recently giving the green light to the Jackdaw gas field after years of uncertainty and a court case.

Pressed further about his previous remarks on Rosebank, Miliband said: "I'm a member of the government and I will abide by collective responsibility on this."

He went on to say there are "direct and very bad impacts at home" for the cost of living linked to Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the Iran conflict.

Miliband added: "What does that teach us? That we can't get economic and energy security from fossil fuels, we've got to keep on with this transition to wind power, solar power, nuclear power; homegrown clean energy we can control."

Catherine Fookes is among a group of Labour MPs, reported to number at least 75, who have signed a letter opposing Rosebank.

The MP for Monmouthshire told Today: "We need to really look at what we're doing and ensure we don't exacerbate our climate challenges and make climate change worse.

"And that's exactly what drilling in the North Sea would do."

Steve Yemm, Labour MP for Mansfield, offered his support to Rosebank and said it would be a "test of whether, as a country, we can support investment and skilled work in the North Sea whilst meeting our climate obligations".

One Labour MP, who is pro Rosebank, said they were increasingly confident the decision would go their way, but added the "gloves will now come off" after Fookes's intervention.

They said people on both sides of the argument had been attempting to avoid so-called "red on red" clashes but predicted Labour MPs would now start to disagree more forcefully in public about the issue.

The same MP accused Miliband of "running two departments" and said the current group of energy ministers were "all his people" and "all coming from the same place".

They said they were becoming increasingly frustrated with Labour MPs who opposed Rosebank and added "Trump is right, we do need to open the North Sea".

Some people in Parliament believe that a decision on the oil field could be made as soon as the end of this month.

Rosebank is Britain's largest untapped oil field and would also produce some gas. It is about 80 miles (128km) north-west of Shetland.

In 2023, the then Conservative UK government granted a licence for Rosebank and a legal challenge followed.

The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that the government had made the approval unlawfully, leaving the current Labour government to make a new decision on whether to give the go-ahead.

If approved, Rosebank is expected to fill up to 500m barrels of oil over its 25-year lifetime.

But prices are determined by international markets, which means there is no guarantee that increased supply would result in cheaper energy bills in the UK.

Environmental campaigners believe approval of Rosebank would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and would have no meaningful impact on the UK's energy security or bills.

They have also argued that Rosebank would be even more damaging for the environment than Jackdaw, as it would produce far more planet-warming greenhouse gases.

The UK is committed to reaching net zero by 2050 - meaning the UK must cut carbon emissions until it removes as much as it produces - and wants to limit global warming to no more than 1.5C above the pre-industrial period.

On Monday, it was announced that gas has begun flowing from the Jackdaw gas field .

Conservative shadow energy secretary Andrew Bowie said: "One gas field does not make an energy strategy.

"Labour cannot claim to back the North Sea while continuing to block new licences, undermine investor confidence, and hammer the industry with a punishing windfall tax."

Bowie added "it is clear that Labour cannot be trusted to deliver the energy security we need" with some of the party's MPs "seemingly poised to rebel" over the approval of Rosebank.

stories.title: Faisal Islam: What's in the Brexit reset food deal and are there trade-offs?
stories.summary: EU minister Hamish Falconer insists Britain would have some influence on policy as part of a new deal.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Some British sausages have faced barriers to being exported to the EU

Published 15 November 2026

In Boston, Lincolnshire, a supplier of ready meals to Marks & Spencer (M&S) manufactures thousands of portions of spaghetti bolognese to be sent to the retailer's shops in the Republic of Ireland.

Every plastic pallet is meticulously individually tagged with a green-grey label “Eire”.

It has been this way since Brexit.

Every truck full of food sent to European Union countries requires hundreds of pages of forms, checks by vets, expense and delays.

It has cost M&S millions of pounds and is part of that reason the British business shut down 11 French stores in 2021.

Many smaller exporters stopped sending their goods to the EU entirely. Some produce, including sausages and certain types of seafood, were entirely stopped.

All this was the predictable consequence of former Prime Minister Boris Johnson’s 2020 deal prioritising regulatory freedom over freeflowing goods trade.

That will end with a Brexit "reset" that Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to sign with the EU on Friday.

The government claims it could boost the economy to the tune of £5bn a year and cut the cost of food for households.

But will the agreement mean a return to frictionless trade for food with the EU or are there trade-offs and quid pro quos the UK will have to make?

EU affairs minister Hamish Falconer, who is a key negotiator with the bloc, acknowledged a “choice” is being made.

In exchange for being able to export produce such as Lincolnshire sausages to the 27 countries, the flipside is the extent to which the UK will be able to influence EU food policies.

The UK will have a "voice in the room", said Falconer, but no vote. Critics have said a reset will make the UK "a rule taker", not a rule maker.

But Falconer said the UK will be involved in a process to shape the rules.

Exit clause

A Brexit reset would not involve any upfront payments, said Falconer, but made it clear there could well be an "exit clause" in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment.

He said this was "reasonable" to consider what would happen if a future Conservative or Reform government wanted to undo the new arrangements. Both parties have said they would if they were in power.

"The EU is worried about that and you can see why," he said.

The BBC understands that the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place following Brexit.

The reset means they will be dismantled.

The prime minister has said he believes there is a "win-win" deal to be had with the EU.

Speaking at a Marks & Spencer food court in central London, Falconer said reducing the cost of importing food "will mean less cost for supermarkets, and I hope that less cost then turns into cheaper produce on the shelves".

He said companies have to currently deal with "pages and pages" of form-filling.

Some exports are rejected for having the wrong colour of ink on forms, or an inaccurate Latin name for cooked meats.

The reset could also mean "tearing up" checks that were introduced on goods flowing from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, following Brexit, he said, as well as separate "Not for EU" labelling.

The whole deal to be signed on Friday is calculated to add 0.4% to UK GDP.

Minister for EU relations Hamish Falconer

Tom Bradshaw, president of the National Farmers' Union, welcomed reduced border inspections and paperwork but said that for the NFU it was "a moment of opportunity and risk" with farmers waiting to see what carve-outs and transitional arrangements would be included.

Trade volumes in food exports to the EU had "fallen significantly - by over a third" since 2019, he said.

But the UK should take a "pragmatic" approach to implementing any new rules.

He raised pesticides and precision breeding - or gene edited crops - as areas where he hoped some compromise would be found.

UK firms are, for example, developing tomatoes engineered to contain extra vitamin D.

Historically the EU has had much stricter rules on gene-editing, but this year relaxed regulations.

Falconer said people would have to "wait and see the detail" in this area.

Contentious crisp flavourings

Another contentious area has been crisp flavourings, with concerns raised that stricter EU rules on certain ingredients might limit the sale of some popular snack flavours in the UK.

"I want to take this opportunity to absolutely stamp down on misinformation about smoky bacon crisps," Falconer said.

Post-Brexit the UK had stayed "pretty closely aligned" to European food safety standards, he said.

Two leading snack brands had already adapted their recipes to accommodate EU rules, an example of the kind of alignment that would happen whether or not there was a reset of UK-EU relations.

"The truth is, almost every business in this country that wants to export food or drink will be aligning with EU rules because it's our biggest market.

"Lots of people, like the good people at Walkers and Frazzles have made these changes already, so I would want to reassure people, particularly smoky bacon fans, it's okay," he said.

stories.title: Create more jobs for under-25s by cutting National Insurance, key report urges
stories.summary: Some parents are so desperate for their children to find a job that they've offered to pay their wages, one hairdresser has told the BBC.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

Salon owner: 'We have parents offering to pay their kids' wages'

Published 15 November 2026

National Insurance (NI) paid by firms on under-25s should be gradually lowered to help create more jobs, a major report will urge.

There are nearly one million 16-24 year-olds not in employment, education or training (Neets) in the UK, official figures show.

Reducing NI costs for firms starting with retail and hospitality firms - which provide almost 40% of jobs for these people - will help improve their opportunities, the report will suggest.

Collette Osborne, a hairdresser who owns two salons in Nottingham, said she feels "suffocated by employment costs" including NI and while she used to employ eight apprentices a year, now she cannot afford to take on any.

Alan Milburn's report will also make recommendations on cutting the benefits bill

Her workforce has more than halved to 21 staff. Osborne told the BBC it costs "around £60,000 to train an apprentice before we can actually start allowing them onto customers' heads".

She said she has had parents so desperate for their children to find employment at her salons that some have even offered to pay their wages.

"I'm inundated with applications - and I mean inundated - which is heartbreaking because I can't take them on," she said.

Osborne does not feel she is getting help to offer jobs to youngsters.

"I feel like the government's foot is firmly on my neck," she said. "They promise breathing space. I feel suffocated, suffocated by employment costs."

The independent report by former Labour minister Alan Milburn has been in the works for a year and will be published on Tuesday in full.

He has already unveiled some of his proposals including:

Reducing benefits - under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide Universal Credit or personal independence payment (Pip), which is the main disability benefit in England and Wales

A legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support with those who refuse to take up potentially losing their benefits.

Doubling the threshold at which businesses start paying NI for 21 to 24-year-olds from £5,000 to £10,000.

At the moment, businesses pay no employer NI contributions for workers younger than 21 or for apprentices under 25 – unless they earn above a threshold of £50,270.

However, for non-apprentices aged 21-24, employers pay 15% on annual earnings above £5,000.

This has been the situation since April 2025, after the then Chancellor Rachel Reeves increased the rate from 13.8% and lowered the threshold from £9,100.

Under Sir Keir Starmer, the government raised NI for firms but Milburn will say the Neets issue was not started by the increase.

Immediately axing NI for 21 to 24-year-olds would cost £5.1bn, according to research by the Resolution Foundation, a left-leaning think tank.

Milburn is set to say that an immediate across-the-board cut in employer NI is not the best use of several billions of pounds of public money.

But shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, said the government should "just stop doing the taxing".

Milburn told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg programme he supported the government subsidising wages to encourage businesses to take on young workers.

"Because young people today are walking into the workplace often with a mental health problem, ADHD or anxiety, if you're a small business that's a cost that you've got to absorb," he said.

"The state has a responsibility to help them with that."

On Sunday, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said the government would extend its subsidised jobs guarantee scheme for 18 to 24-year-olds who are claiming Universal Credit.

People who have been on benefits for 12 months will be eligible, down from 18 months and the scheme would be available for people in England, Scotland and Wales.

McFadden said the scheme, which guarantees workers a six-month job, "will help more than 90,000 young people into work by March 2029".

stories.title: Amazon Ring’s New Indoor Surveillance Drone Is Not Compatible with Privacy
stories.summary: Amazon Ring has finally announced their long-dreaded indoor drone , a small flying surveillance device connected to their security suite of products that can fly around your house filming and recording things. The device is supposedly designed to fly preset paths across your home and will also activate if a sensor or alarm has been triggered. Customers should think twice about purchasing these devices for a number of reasons. These devices are problematic in many of the ways we’ve said Ring’s stationary home surveillance products are a problem , plus some new ways. At a very basic level, they are essentially a window into your house that can be accessed by anyone with access to your account—which has historically included bad actors looking to embarrass or harass Ring users and employees of the company . What’s worse, Ring has supercharged the units with its ‘AI Pilot’ to map routes, model the interior of the home, and control movement. This means not only is the footage being sent to corporate servers, but the company is also making inferences about your home to carry out tasks. How much home usage data this is based on, and if it can be used to infer when certain household activities are happening, are both open questions. And presumably, to maintain the preset routes, inferred data about your home will still be held by Ring even after any stored video footage is deleted. The risk to your privacy is only compounded once you consider Ring’s renewed partnership with police through the massive surveillance and taser vendor, Axon. Through this partnership, police have the ability to request camera footage from Ring users with just a few clicks on Axon’s platforms. This includes its Fusus platform , an interactive surveillance feed and map police use to manage all the surveillance devices they have access to, like automated license plate readers . It’s unclear exactly what devices police can request footage from, but if this request feature is extended to Ring’s drones, police could easily send requests for footage from inside your house. Sharing is voluntary, but once footage is submitted, it cannot be retracted.
